chapter: Depression years and New Orleans trumpeters
title: Professions and the interviewer's own path
summary: Small talk about musicians who worked through college, the interviewer's pre-med years and arrival in New Orleans in 1945 with Monk Hazel, and first hearing Harry Shields.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: My family were all doctors. Is that right? But I wasn't following.
Well, I'll tell you, it's nothing like having a profession.
Did you, in going back to some of your work and what you're doing, you're not following in journalism?
We're supervised by the history department.
We even have one of our teachers over there plays clarinet and saxophone.

Many do. Many played their way through universities with black sticks. Mm-hmm. We had a very dear friend during the World War II days in Valparaiso, Florida. One of the men has done a lot of research in the Rubin method of child delivery. He was Dr. Arthur David. He's, he played his way playing basketball and clarinet. That's how he worked his way through college. Mm-hmm. That's a fight. Or through medical school. And that's a very difficult thing to do. You know that yourself. I know. Or as your parents and your family can tell you.
I even went to medical school all while myself. But I didn't like it.
Did you have two years pre-med?
I had a degree in pre-med.
And then I went into medical school and didn't like it. Decided I wanted to get in the music business. Came to New Orleans. I came down to New Orleans in 1945 in the Navy and I met Monk. Oh, I see.
And he told me where to go and I went around.
That's when I first heard Harry Shields.
